b2017-1.ask: Cards show 2 0 1 7. Which row can you NOT get by swapping just two cards?
steps: One swap moves exactly two cards. Every other card stays in its spot.
For each choice, count how many cards are in a different spot from 2 0 1 7.
If exactly 2 cards moved (and they traded places), one swap works.
0 1 2 7: the 2, 0 and 1 have all moved. That's 3 cards, so one swap can't do it.
b2017-1.check: The others: 2 7 1 0 swaps 0 and 7, 1 0 2 7 swaps 2 and 1, 0 2 1 7 swaps 2 and 0, 2 0 7 1 swaps 1 and 7. ✓
b2017-1.spot: Which one can't happen? Pretend each is possible and look for a broken rule.
b2017-1.oops: Only checking whether the same digits are used.

b2017-2.ask: 3 flies (6 legs) and 2 spiders (8 legs) have as many legs as 9 chickens and how many cats?
steps: Flies and spiders: 3 × 6 + 2 × 8 = 18 + 16 = 34 legs.
9 chickens: 9 × 2 = 18 legs.
Legs still needed: 34 − 18 = 16.
Cats have 4 legs: 16 ÷ 4 = 4 cats.
b2017-2.spot: Two sides that must balance? Work out both sides, then fill the gap.

b2017-3.ask: Alice has 4 straight pieces, each 3 squares long. Which picture can't she make?
steps: Each picture uses 12 squares (4 × 3). Check each one can be cut into straight pieces of 3.
Start at awkward spots: a square at the very end of a row can often be covered only one way.
In picture E, the leftmost and rightmost squares can only be covered by pieces lying sideways.
Once those two pieces are placed, the squares left over don't make a straight line of 3. So E is impossible.
b2017-3.check: For each of the other pictures you can draw the 4 straight pieces. ✓
b2017-3.spot: Covering with pieces? Start with the square that has only one way to be covered.
b2017-3.oops: Only checking that there are 12 squares.

b2017-4.check: Double each digit of 1234321: 2, 4, 6, 8, 6, 4, 2. ✓ (No carrying needed.)
b2017-4.spot: A new problem close to one you know? Use the known answer.

b2017-5.ask: Islands are joined by bridges. Fewest bridges to close so no one can travel from A to B?
steps: Look for separate routes from A to B that don't share any bridge.
Each separate route needs at least one closed bridge.
There are 2 routes that don't share bridges, so at least 2 closures.
And closing 2 well-chosen bridges does cut A off from B.
b2017-5.check: After closing those 2, try every path from A: none reaches B. ✓
b2017-5.spot: Cutting all paths? Count the routes that don't share anything.
b2017-5.oops: Closing bridges far away from where the routes come together.

b2017-6.ask: Jane walks in front, Kate in the middle, Lynn behind. Jane is 500 kg heavier than Kate. Kate is 1000 kg lighter than Lynn. Which picture is right?
steps: Kate is the lightest (Jane and Lynn are both heavier than her).
Lynn is 1000 kg more than Kate, Jane 500 kg more. So Lynn is the heaviest.
Order: front (Jane) medium, middle (Kate) small, back (Lynn) big.
Picture A shows medium, small, big.
b2017-6.check: Small Kate between them, biggest one at the back. ✓
b2017-6.spot: Who's heavier? Put them in order from the clues, then match.
b2017-6.oops: Reading 'Kate weighs 1000 kg less' as Kate being heavier.

b2017-7.ask: Opposite faces of a die all have the same sum. Five faces are 5, 6, 9, 11, 14. What's the sixth?
steps: The three opposite pairs all have the same sum.
Look for two pairs among the known numbers that match: 6 + 14 = 20 and 9 + 11 = 20.
So the leftover, 5, must pair with the missing number to make 20 too.
b2017-7.spot: Equal pairs? Look for two pairs that match; the odd one out tells you the rest.
b2017-7.oops: Assuming the missing number is the smallest.

b2017-8.ask: A rectangle of 18 squares: 1/3 blue, 1/2 yellow, the rest red. How many red?
steps: Blue: 1/3 of 18 = 6 squares.
Yellow: 1/2 of 18 = 9 squares.
b2017-8.spot: Fractions of a group? Turn each fraction into a number first.
b2017-8.oops: Counting the squares wrong. 3 rows of 6 = 18.

b2017-9.ask: Nick solves 3 problems while Peter solves 2. Together they solved 30. How many more did Nick solve?
steps: Every 'round', Peter solves 2 and Nick solves 3: 5 problems.
30 ÷ 5 = 6 rounds.
b2017-9.spot: 'In the time it takes...'? Group them into rounds.

b2017-10.ask: Bob folded paper and punched one hole. Unfolded, it has holes in a diagonal line. Which fold lines did he use?
steps: Each fold stacks layers on top of each other. One punch makes a hole through every layer.
Unfolding mirrors the hole across each fold line. So the fold lines must cross the row of holes at right angles, like mirrors.
Fold once across the middle of the row: 4 holes become 2. Fold again across the middle of what's left: 2 holes become 1.
So the folds are lines that cut straight across the diagonal row of holes. That's picture D.
b2017-10.check: Fold paper along D's lines, punch once, unfold: holes in a diagonal row. ✓
b2017-10.spot: Punched holes? Unfold step by step, mirroring the hole each time.
b2017-10.oops: Picking folds that would put holes in a cross or a square pattern.

b2017-11.ask: A sofa (3 pieces + armrests) is 220 cm, a loveseat (2 pieces + armrests) is 160 cm. How wide is a chair (1 piece + armrests)?
steps: Sofa and loveseat have the same armrests. The sofa has one extra middle piece.
220 − 160 = 60 cm. So one piece is 60 cm.
Loveseat: 2 pieces = 120 cm, so the armrests together are 160 − 120 = 40 cm.
b2017-11.spot: Things built from the same parts? Compare two and the difference is one part.

b2017-13.ask: From 1234567891011121314151617181920, delete 24 digits so the remaining 7-digit number is as big as possible.
steps: Keep 7 digits. The first digit matters most, so make it as big as possible: a 9.
There's a 9 early (the single 9) and a 9 in 19. Take the first 9 to leave enough digits after it.
After the 9, keep picking the biggest digit that still leaves enough digits to reach 7 in total: 7, then 8, then 1, 9, 2, 0.
That gives 9781920.
b2017-13.check: It's 7 digits, they appear in this order in the long number, and no bigger choice works at any step. ✓
b2017-13.spot: Biggest number from digits in order? Pick the biggest digit you can at each step, leaving enough digits for the rest.
b2017-13.oops: Grabbing a 9 too late, so there aren't enough digits left.

b2017-15.ask: In a 2 × 2 grid with a, b on top and c, d below, the rows add to 2 and 3, the columns to 1 and 4. Which is true?
steps: Write the sums: a + b = 2 (top row) and b + d = 4 (right column).
Both have b. Take it off both: d is 2 more than a.
So a is less than d.
b2017-15.answer: D: a is less than d.
b2017-15.check: An example: a = 0, b = 2, c = 1, d = 2. Rows 2 and 3 ✓, columns 1 and 4 ✓, and a < d ✓.
b2017-15.spot: Two sums sharing a number? Take away what they share.
b2017-15.oops: Trying to find exact values. You only need to compare.

b2017-16.ask: Peter hiked 5 days, 2 km more each day, 70 km total. How far on Thursday?
steps: Wednesday is the middle day. Monday is 4 less, Friday 4 more; Tuesday 2 less, Thursday 2 more. They balance out.
So the total = 5 × Wednesday.
70 ÷ 5 = 14 km on Wednesday.
Thursday = 14 + 2 = 16 km.
b2017-16.spot: Numbers going up evenly? The middle one is the average.

b2017-17.ask: Each shared side between triangles is a mirror. A kangaroo picture gets reflected from triangle to triangle. What does it look like in the shaded triangle?
steps: Each reflection flips the picture over the shared side.
Two reflections in a row turn the picture around (no longer mirrored).
Keep reflecting one triangle at a time until you reach the shaded one, drawing each step.
The shaded triangle shows picture E.
b2017-17.check: Count the reflections: an odd number gives a mirrored kangaroo, and E is mirrored the right way. ✓
b2017-17.spot: Repeated reflections? Draw each one step by step.
b2017-17.oops: Skipping steps and losing track of which way it faces.

b2017-18.ask: Wands: +1 dollar, −1 dollar, ×2. Each used once. Which order gives the most money?
steps: Doubling makes everything bigger, so double when you have the most.
Add 1 BEFORE doubling: the extra dollar gets doubled too.
Subtract 1 AFTER doubling: then you only lose 1 dollar, not 2.
Order: +1, ×2, −1. You end with 2 × (money + 1) − 1 = 2 × money + 1.
b2017-18.check: Start with 5: +1, ×2, −1 → 6, 12, 11. Any other order gives less (like −1, ×2, +1 → 4, 8, 9). ✓
b2017-18.spot: Order of steps? Test with a small starting number.
b2017-18.oops: Doubling first, so the +1 doesn't get doubled.

b2017-19.ask: Three squares (sides 2, 4, 6) overlap, each corner at the centre of the one before. What's the total shaded area?
steps: Where two squares overlap, that bit got counted twice.
A corner at the centre of a square covers a quarter of it. First overlap: 1/4 of the small square = 1. Second: 1/4 of the middle square = 4.
b2017-19.spot: Overlapping shapes? Add them all, then take away the overlaps counted twice.
b2017-19.oops: Adding the three areas and stopping at 56.

b2017-21.ask: Each bar is 2 gray cubes + 1 white cube in a row. Which big cube can be built from 9 bars?
steps: Every bar is 3 cubes in a straight line: gray, gray, white (white at one end). So no bar has white in the middle.
In each picture, look for a cube that can't belong to ANY bar: in every direction its line of 3 has the wrong colours.
In B, C and D you can find such a cube: every line through it has two or three white cubes, but a bar has only one.
E fails a sneakier way: the centre of the front face and the centre of the right face would both need the big cube's centre. Only A works.
b2017-21.check: In A, lay all 9 bars side to side; each one shows its white or gray end on the right face. ✓
b2017-21.spot: Building from pieces? Look for one spot no piece could fill.
b2017-21.oops: Only counting gray and white cubes (18 and 9) without checking the arrangement.

b2017-22.ask: Put 1 to 5 in the cells so numbers below are bigger and numbers to the right are bigger. How many ways?
steps: The top-left cell has cells below and to the right, so it must be the smallest: 1.
5 is the biggest, so it can only go at an end: the far right cell or the bottom cell.
If 5 is at the far right, there are 3 ways to place 2, 3 and 4 that follow the rules.
If 5 is at the bottom, it's the same picture flipped: 3 more ways. 3 + 3 = 6.
b2017-22.check: Each arrangement you listed obeys both rules, and none is repeated. ✓
b2017-22.spot: Placing numbers with 'bigger than' rules? Place the smallest and biggest first.
b2017-22.oops: Missing some arrangements by not listing in order.

b2017-23.ask: 8 kangaroos face left or right. Two facing each other can swap by jumping. How many swaps happen until no more are possible?
steps: Swaps only happen when a right-facing kangaroo is just left of a left-facing one.
In the end, all left-facing kangaroos will have passed all right-facing ones that were in front of them.
So each left-facing kangaroo jumps once for every right-facing kangaroo that started to its left.
Count them for each left-facing kangaroo: 3 + 5 + 5 = 13.
b2017-23.check: Each swap passes exactly one pair, and there are 13 pairs to pass. ✓
b2017-23.spot: Things passing each other? Count how many each one must pass.
b2017-23.oops: Trying to act out every jump and losing track.

b2017-24.ask: Monica picks 5 different numbers and multiplies each by 2 or 3. What's the fewest different results she can get?
steps: To get the same result twice, one number × 2 must equal another number × 3. Example: 3 × 2 = 6 and 2 × 3 = 6.
Each result can come from at most 2 of the numbers (one doubled, one tripled).
So 5 numbers need at least 3 results: two matching pairs and one number on its own.
And 3 is possible, as the check shows.
b2017-24.spot: Making things equal? Find pairs that match, then pair up as many as you can.
b2017-24.oops: Thinking you can get 1 or 2 results. Each result can come from at most 2 of the numbers.

b2017-25.ask: A floor has gray and white tiles (triangles and squares). Fewest gray tiles to swap with white tiles so the floor looks the same from all four sides?
steps: Swapping keeps the same number of gray tiles: 4 gray triangles and 4 gray squares (with 8 white of each).
To look the same from all four sides, each edge must look the same. 4 gray triangles on 4 edges means 1 gray and 2 white triangles per edge, in the same order: gray, white, white.
Swapping one white triangle on the right edge with the gray middle triangle on the bottom edge fixes the triangles.
For the squares, one swap makes the middle all white and each edge white-then-gray. Total: one triangle and one square.
b2017-25.check: After the two swaps, turn the picture a quarter turn: it looks the same. ✓
b2017-25.spot: Same from every side? Turn the picture in your head and compare.
b2017-25.oops: Recolouring tiles instead of swapping them. A swap keeps the number of gray tiles the same.

b2017-27.ask: Ala takes even numbers, Beata multiples of 3, Celina multiples of 5. Each takes all the balls she likes when it's her turn. Who went in what order?
steps: Beata got 45. 45 is also a multiple of 5, so Celina would have taken it if she went first. So Beata went before Celina.
Celina got 20. 20 is even, so Ala would have taken it if she went first. So Celina went before Ala.
Order: Beata, Celina, Ala.
b2017-27.check: Beata takes 24, 33, 45. Celina takes 20, 25, 35. Ala takes 32, 52. ✓
b2017-27.spot: Who went first? Look at things that more than one person wanted.
b2017-27.oops: Ignoring that some balls fit two girls' rules.

b2017-29.ask: Julia colours a map of 4 countries with up to 4 colours. Touching countries must differ. How many ways?
steps: Colour the country that touches the most others first: 4 choices.
Its neighbour: 3 choices (anything but the first colour).
The next country touches both: 2 choices.
The last country doesn't touch one of the others, so it has 2 choices. 4 × 3 × 2 × 2 = 48.
b2017-29.check: Multiply the choices at each step. ✓
b2017-29.spot: Colouring with choices? Colour the busiest country first and multiply the choices.
b2017-29.oops: Thinking every country touches every other (4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24).

b2017-30.ask: On a 6 × 6 board, a lamp lights up when 2 lit neighbours share a corner with it. Fewest lamps to light at the start so eventually all light up?
steps: A new lamp lights only when it sits in the corner between two lit lamps, like filling in an L-shape to make a square.
Draw the outline around the lit lamps. When a new lamp lights up, the outline never gets longer (it stays the same or shrinks).
A fully lit 6 × 6 board has an outline of 24. Each lamp lit at the start adds at most 4 to the outline.
So you need at least 24 ÷ 4 = 6 lamps. And 6 lamps on a diagonal do light up everything.
b2017-30.check: Start with the diagonal lit: the squares between neighbours fill in, step by step, until all 36 are lit. ✓
b2017-30.spot: Things spreading? Look for something that can never grow, then see what's the least you need.
